# Closed-Loop Execution and Ownership


When transitioning from technical foundations to full-system operation, the central challenge shifts from point AI assistance on isolated tasks to operating and evaluating complete, closed-loop design systems. Part III runs design loops as far as execution records take them, reports where execution stops, measures what transfers across design problems, and evaluates automated workflows against matched baselines without falling prey to confirmation bias.

This operational transition confronts the tension between *Empirical Honesty and Unearned Claims*. An automated study that halts at early simulation and records unverified thermal boundaries is an architectural success; an unverified claim of end-to-end tapeout is a failure of discipline. These chapters examine how closed-loop exploration operates across multi-fidelity tools, how requalification contracts bound negative transfer, and what total-cost accounting and red-teaming defenses must establish before an AI-native design system can claim credible empirical support. The part closes by separating what evidence supports from what a named architect backed by an accountable organization decides to commit, returning to the Lighthouse prompt to state plainly what the study results establish and what they leave open.

::: {.callout-part}
1. How can design teams execute staged evaluation loops that reject unsound proposals before incurring expensive physical design costs?
2. What governance frameworks ensure that automated tool decisions preserve human architectural ownership and commitment authority?
:::

| **@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack** | What design mechanisms and offload bounds generalize across distinct hardware problems? | Formulates LogCA offload bounds, requalification contracts, and Triton-to-RVV 1.0 lowering paths. |
